Indoctrination

/in-dok-trih-NAY-shun/ - the stress falls on NAY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Indoctrination means the teaching of a set of beliefs so thoroughly that they are accepted without question.

The sect's catechism ran to ninety questions, and indoctrination began with the first: every answer given word for word, or repeated until it was.

Worked Example

The movement's summer camps photographed beautifully: lakes, campfires, hiking badges. The schedule told another story. A song at reveille, a song before meals, an oath before swimming; every badge stitched with a slogan, every ghost story ending in the founder's rescue. Veterans of those summers could still sing every verse fifty years on — and could not recall one evening when anyone had asked what the verses meant.

Indoctrination is the exact word for those camps, because indoctrination means the teaching of a set of beliefs so thoroughly that they are accepted without question — the missing questions are the tell. Education hands you the beliefs and the tools to test them; indoctrination hands you the beliefs and quietly takes the tools.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

conditioning: trains responses the body gives before thought; indoctrination trains the thoughts themselves

brainwashing: the violent extreme — a mind emptied and refilled; indoctrination is slower and wears a school's face

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

education: hands over the tools of doubt along with the facts

inquiry: starts from the very questions indoctrination removes

Where it sits · how much independent questioning survives — instruction → indoctrination → brainwashing

instruction vs. indoctrination: Instruction simply hands the material over — the manual, the drill, the theorem — and welcomes a raised hand.

brainwashing vs. indoctrination: Brainwashing goes further than indoctrination — the indoctrinated student has stopped asking questions; the brainwashed one can no longer form them.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, into

Root — doctrin

Root — doctrin: teaching, body of beliefs (Latin doctrina)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the act or process of

Put it together

Put it together: In- (into) + doctrin (teaching) + -ation (the process of) = the process of driving a teaching in. Latin doctrina is the taught thing itself, from docere, to teach — and the in- tells you how far it goes: not set before the student, but pressed into the student until it will not come back out.

Use the root in a new word: doctor

Use the root in a new word: doctor: A doctor was originally a teacher — Latin docere; universities still say doctorate — and the healing sense arrived centuries later.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / critical

Indoctrination is an accusation about method: the beliefs may even be true, but they were installed, not examined. Propaganda is its outward-facing cousin — posters aimed at strangers, while indoctrination drills its own. And do not let the spelling pull you toward this unit's induce: induce leads (Latin ducere), indoctrination teaches (docere) — look-alike prefixes on unrelated roots.
